item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
attempts at synthesizing more of what is thought to be the active ingredient of the pills have been unsuccessful.

Most methods in analytical chemistry and structure elucidation are inherently destructive. So testing will be limited. This gives us a few possibilities.

A) They haven't identified exactly what part of the pill is the active ingredient. I recall reading a study where a team attempted to synthesize a chemical from a natural source that had shown promising results in trials. After years of work, the chemical was made, and… nothing. Apparently the true medical power was from a trace component of the natural sample.

B) They cannot elucidate the structure/formula of the active ingredient. For highly complex organic molecules, identification of unknown compounds can be difficult. Couple that with the classic "SCP gives a bizarre reading on instruments", and now you have an NMR spectrum with peaks where peaks cannot be, or other such headaches.

C) They have the structure, or something close to it, but it's incredibly hard to synthesize. Nonanomalous chemical synthesis is already a nightmare for some compounds we understand well. If this thing has some bizarre or (supposedly) unstable structure, like a pentavalent carbon or a set of three-membered rings connected by peroxides (I'm talking out of my ass here), then they're gonna have a hard time barring the use of some sort of chemical paratech.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Also, they can't synthesize it. It's a problem we have with certain real-world proteins, like spidersilk: it's one thing to know what they're made of and how they fit together. It's a whole different thing to be able to produce it without the spider.

It is literally easier to genetically engineer goats to express the spidersilk protein in their milk and extract it from solution than to design an industrial process that can produce useful amounts of spidersilk. And that's when you start with a gene providing the schematic to tell cells how to construct it- here they don't even have that.

item.title: Re: Something I just thought of
item.content:encoded:
Ideas are great and you should keep them coming. Voct's point is more that part of the idea of SCP-500 is "the fear of indecision":

  • You have three wishes - what do you do?
  • You are immortal and can make ONE other person immortal - who do you choose? Or do you wait and maybe find one other person immortal?
  • You can can cure ANYONE of ANYTHING… 47 times. Do you give it to a child and hope they go on to do great things - instead of the next Hitler? Do you give it to Stephan Hawking and hope he continues to do great work instead of renouncing science and becoming a televangelist preaching about his miracle cure?

It's meant to show the fear of becoming like many lottery winners/music starts/etc. They wind up in debt after they hit it big because they made poor choices.

item.title: Something I just thought of
item.content:encoded:
What if… whenever all the pills are used up… the bottle refills itself with another 60 pills? This has always been part of its anomaly, but the Foundation never learns this, because they're too scared to waste the pills.

The years go by… over and over, people die horribly who could have been saved by a dose of -500. Every few decades, someone convinces the Foundation to use JUST! ONE! PILL! PLEASE! JUST THIS ONCE!, and the remaining pills are kept under even tighter control as a result…

… and all along, if the Foundation would just use them generously to help everyone possible, they'd keep getting refills.

I'm imagining, millennia in the future, a meeting of the O5 council… squabbling over who gets to use the last SCP-500 pill. And then shots are fired. All the centuries-old O5s are killed, except one. He grabs the last SCP-500 pill, and gulps it down, and his many and various illnesses are all healed…

… and then the bottle goes CLICK CLUNK, and it's refilled.

And he stares at it in horror…

… and a piece of ceiling falls on him and kills him dead.
